title: Chemicals in Everyday Plastics Linked to High Blood Pressure During Pregnancy
excerpt: New research finds phthalates — endocrine-disrupting chemicals found in food packaging, personal care products and household plastics — may contribute to hypertensive disorders in pregnant women.
body:
• Phthalates, chemicals found in plastics and personal care products, are linked to elevated blood pressure during pregnancy
  • The research published by the Endocrine Society found these endocrine-disrupting chemicals may interfere with placental hormones critical for healthy pregnancies
  • Women who developed pregnancy complications like gestational diabetes and high blood pressure showed stronger associations with phthalate exposure
  • Experts say reducing exposure requires both individual awareness and broader regulatory action

Phthalates — a group of chemicals used to make plastics more flexible and found in everything from food packaging to personal care products — may contribute to high blood pressure in pregnant women, according to new research highlighted by the Endocrine Society.

The findings add to a growing body of evidence that these endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) can interfere with hormonal processes during pregnancy, potentially affecting both maternal and fetal health.

How Phthalates Affect Pregnancy

Research from Rutgers University, published in Environment International, examined how phthalate exposure affects placental corticotropin-releasing hormone (pCRH), a hormone produced by the placenta that increases throughout pregnancy. When pCRH levels are abnormally high or rise too rapidly, it can contribute to preterm birth, fetal growth problems, high blood pressure, diabetes and postpartum depression.

"Our findings show that these chemicals may alter the production of essential placental hormones, which has important implications for the course of pregnancy as well as subsequent child health and development."

— Emily S. Barrett, Rutgers School of Public Health

The study analysed data from 1,018 low-risk pregnant women carrying single fetuses at two time points during pregnancy. Researchers found that phthalate exposure was associated with higher pCRH levels in mid-pregnancy but lower levels later — a pattern that was most pronounced in women who developed complications like gestational diabetes and hypertension.

Exposure Is Nearly Universal

Phthalates enter the body through diet, skin absorption and inhalation. They are present in plastic food containers, children's toys, vinyl flooring, detergents, cosmetics, nail polish and many pharmaceutical coatings. Unlike persistent organic pollutants, phthalates break down relatively quickly in the body, but constant daily exposure means levels remain consistently elevated.

"People are exposed to phthalates daily, increasing their risk of several metabolic diseases," said Sung Kyun Park of the University of Michigan School of Public Health, who has studied phthalate exposure and diabetes risk. "It's important that we address EDCs now as they are harmful to human health."

Beyond Blood Pressure

The cardiovascular risks of phthalate exposure extend beyond pregnancy. Research published in the Endocrine Society's Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism found that phthalate exposure was associated with a 30-63% higher chance of developing diabetes in certain populations. Separate animal studies have shown that exposure to related chemicals like bisphenol A (BPA) can significantly increase both systolic and diastolic blood pressure in offspring.

The connection between maternal chemical exposure and infant health outcomes is also being investigated. Studies suggest that phthalates may affect infant gut microbiota development and influence growth patterns in the months after birth.

Reducing Exposure

While individual steps can help — such as avoiding plastic food storage, choosing fragrance-free personal care products and reducing processed food consumption — experts emphasise that meaningful change requires regulatory action. Phthalates remain widely used in consumer products across the globe, and pregnant women may not be aware of the extent of their exposure.

For expecting mothers, the research underscores the importance of discussing environmental exposures with healthcare providers, particularly during the second and third trimesters when the hormonal effects appear most significant.
nri_angle: Health awareness around chemical exposure during pregnancy is relevant to diaspora families navigating both American consumer products and traditional practices.
